decks.title: Nature and Significance of Management — Part 1: Meaning, Objectives and Characteristics
goals: Explain the four ways in which the term management is understood
List the organisational, social and personal objectives of management
Describe the characteristics of management with examples

slides.heading: Nature and Significance of Management
slides.body_md: Part 1: the four **meanings** of management, its **objectives** and its **characteristics**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the four meanings of management, its objectives and its characteristics
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every organisation, from a village library to a large exporter, needs someone to make sure the work gets done well. That someone, and that work, is management. In this part we see the four ways the word is used, what management tries to achieve, and the features that mark it out.

slides.heading: Four ways to read the word
slides.body_md: **Management** is the process of getting things done **effectively and efficiently** through others, to achieve the goals of an organisation.

rows: What managers do: interpersonal, informational and decisional tasks
The body of persons who manage an organisation
An organised field of study with its own principles
A chain of functions: plan, organise, staff, direct, control
How work moves from idea to result

visual.alt: Table of the four meanings of management: as an activity, a group, a discipline and a process, with what each means and how it is heard

slides.narration: The word management is used in four senses. As an activity, it is what managers do each day. As a group, it means the people who run the organisation. As a discipline, it is a subject we study. As a process, it is a chain of functions that turns plans into results.

slides.heading: Management as a process
slides.body_md: The five functions follow one another, and controlling feeds back into the next plan.

visual.alt: Flow of the five functions of management in order: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling, with controlling feeding back into planning
visual.caption: Controlling feeds back into the next round of planning.

slides.narration: Seen as a process, management begins with planning, deciding in advance what to do. Organising arranges tasks and resources. Staffing fills posts with the right people. Directing guides and motivates them. Controlling compares results with plans, and what it finds becomes the starting point for the next round of planning.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which sense?
slides.body_md: Decide which sense of management each imagined sentence uses.
bullets: Step 1: find the **clue**: people, a subject, a chain of steps, or daily tasks.
Step 2: name the sense.
Step 3: give a one-line reason.

rows: "Management has fixed the new shift timings" (a bakery notice)
"He teaches management at a college in Ranchi"
"First we plan the stall, then we assign volunteers, then we check sales"
"She spent the day meeting suppliers and choosing a vendor"

visual.alt: Worked table: four imagined sentences, the clue in each, and the sense of management it uses
visual.caption: Look for the clue: people, a subject, a chain of steps, or tasks.

slides.narration: Let us practise. A notice saying management has fixed new shift timings refers to people, so it is the group sense. Teaching management at college is the discipline sense. Planning a stall, assigning volunteers and checking sales is a chain of steps, the process sense. Meeting suppliers and choosing a vendor is the activity sense.

slides.heading: Quick check: a field of study
slides.body_md: True or false: management as a discipline means the organised body of knowledge that is taught and studied.
slides.narration: Think about what we mean when we call something a subject of study.

slides.heading: Management as an activity
slides.body_md: Managers spend their day on three kinds of tasks.

rows: Deals with people inside and outside
Meets a buyer; settles a quarrel
Shares news of a craft fair

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of managerial activity, interpersonal, informational and decisional, with an imagined example of each

slides.narration: As an activity, management covers three kinds of work. Interpersonal tasks mean dealing with people, such as meeting a buyer or settling a quarrel. Informational tasks mean collecting and passing on news. Decisional tasks mean making choices, such as which order to accept or how to share a budget.

slides.heading: Objectives of management

rows: A trekking firm cuts costs to stay open in a bad year
Benefit to society: safe products, jobs, clean environment
A seafood exporter treats its waste water
Employees' financial, social and higher-level needs
A spice firm pays for evening classes for workers

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of objectives of management, what each includes and an imagined example

slides.narration: Management works towards three kinds of objectives. Organisational objectives are survival, profit and growth. Social objectives create benefit for society, such as safe products, jobs and a clean environment. Personal objectives meet the needs of employees: fair pay, recognition from others, and the chance to grow.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sorting objectives
slides.body_md: An imagined pickle cooperative in Rajahmundry writes down four aims.
bullets: Step 1: ask **who benefits**: the firm, society or employees.
Step 2: name the kind of objective.
Step 3: for organisational aims, say whether it is survival, profit or growth.

headers: Aim of an imagined pickle cooperative in Rajahmundry
rows: Earn enough in the mango season to last the year
Start selling in two new states
Buy mangoes at fair prices from small growers
Give each member a bonus and a chance to learn bookkeeping

visual.alt: Worked table sorting four aims of an imagined pickle cooperative into organisational, social and personal objectives
visual.caption: Ask: who benefits — the firm, society or the people working in it?

slides.narration: Look at the cooperative's aims. Earning enough in the mango season to last the year is survival. Selling in two new states is growth. Paying fair prices to small growers benefits society, so it is social. A bonus and a chance to learn bookkeeping meet members' own needs, so it is personal.

slides.heading: Quick check: an analogy
slides.body_md: Complete the analogy: earning a surplus over costs is to organisational objective as supplying safe products to the community is to ___ objective.
slides.narration: Who benefits from safe products: the firm, society, or the staff?

slides.heading: Characteristics of management

rows: Found in every kind of organisation and at every level
Its functions repeat without a break
Unites people with different needs towards common goals
Cannot be seen, but its results can be felt

visual.alt: Table of five characteristics of management: goal-oriented, pervasive, continuous, group activity and intangible

slides.narration: Management has five key characteristics. It is goal-oriented, because all its work aims at definite objectives. It is pervasive, found in every kind of organisation. It is continuous, with functions repeating without a break. It is a group activity, uniting people with different needs. And it is intangible: we cannot see it, but we feel its results.

slides.heading: Reading the clues in a case
columns:
**Pervasive**

A kitchen, a ferry cooperative and a start-up all plan and check their work.

**Intangible**

No one sees the organisers, yet the event runs smoothly.

rows: Many different kinds of organisation all plan and check work
Nobody sees the managers, but everything runs smoothly
The next plan starts as soon as one ends

visual.alt: Table of clues in a case and the characteristic each points to: pervasive, intangible and continuous

slides.narration: In case questions, look for clues. When many different kinds of organisation all plan and check their work, the answer is pervasive. When nobody sees the managers but everything runs smoothly, it is intangible. When a new plan begins as soon as one ends, it is continuous.

slides.heading: Quick check: working together
slides.body_md: Dyers, weavers, accountants and sales staff with different needs work together on one export order. Which characteristic is this?
slides.narration: Focus on many different people joining their efforts for one goal.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Goal-oriented, pervasive, continuous, group activity, intangible

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: four meanings, the process, three kinds of objectives and five characteristics

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Management can be read as an activity, a group, a discipline or a process. Its objectives are organisational, social and personal. It is goal-oriented, pervasive, continuous, a group activity and intangible.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **four meanings** and the clue for each.
For objectives, ask **who benefits**.
Name the **exact** characteristic: pervasive, intangible, continuous, group activity or goal-oriented.
In cases, quote the line before naming the idea.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the line, name the idea, and explain the link

slides.narration: A few tips. Learn the four meanings with a clue for each. Sort objectives by asking who benefits. Name characteristics exactly; do not mix up pervasive and continuous. And in every case question, quote the line, name the idea, then explain the link.

decks.title: Nature and Significance of Management — Part 2: Science, Art, Profession, Importance and Levels
goals: Evaluate how far management fulfils the features of a science, an art and a profession
Explain the importance of management for an organisation and for society
Describe the functions of top, middle and supervisory levels of management

slides.heading: Is Management a Science, an Art or a Profession?
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **nature** of management, its **importance**, and the three **levels** of management.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: management as a science, an art and a profession, its importance, and the levels of management
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we ask a famous question: is management a science, an art or a profession? Then we see why management matters to a firm and to society, and finally we meet the three levels of managers who share the work.

slides.heading: Management as a science
slides.body_md: A **science** is a systematised body of knowledge with principles that explain cause and effect.

rows: Principles based on observation and experiment
Yes, though people cannot be tested like chemicals
Only partly: results vary with people and situations

visual.alt: Table of three features of science and how far management has each: systematised knowledge yes, experiment-based principles yes, universal validity only partly
visual.caption: So management is an inexact, or soft, science.

slides.narration: Science has three features. It is a systematised body of knowledge. Its principles come from observation and experiment. And they hold true everywhere. Management has the first two. But because it deals with people, its principles do not give the same result in every place. So management is an inexact, or soft, science.

slides.heading: Management as an art
slides.body_md: An **art** is the skilful and personal application of knowledge to get results.

rows: Many books and principles on managing
Each manager applies them in an own style
Skill grows with practice and fresh ideas

visual.alt: Table of three features of art and how each appears in management

slides.narration: Art also has three features. There is a body of theory to learn. Each artist applies it in a personal way. And skill grows through practice and creativity. Management fits all three: there are many books on managing, each manager has an individual style, and good managers get better with practice.

slides.heading: Management as a profession
slides.body_md: A **profession** is an occupation with special knowledge, restricted entry and a binding code of conduct.

rows: No: anyone can be a manager
Not fully: codes exist but are not binding by law
Partly: firms serve society but mainly pursue their goals

visual.alt: Table of five features of a profession and how far management meets each

slides.narration: A profession such as medicine or law has a body of knowledge, restricted entry through a set degree, a compulsory association, a code of conduct with penalties, and a service motive. Management has a body of knowledge, but anyone may become a manager, membership of an association is voluntary, and codes do not bind managers by law.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: science, art or profession?
slides.body_md: Match each imagined fact with the nature of management it shows.
bullets: Step 1: spot the **feature** in the fact.
Step 2: decide whether management **meets** it.
Step 3: write the verdict.

rows: A tea-shop owner in Indore runs her staff in her own way
A chain tested two shift patterns and kept the better one
A hotel appoints a manager with no management degree
A bonus that worked in Surat fails in Shillong

visual.alt: Worked table matching four imagined facts to art, science, not a full profession, or inexact science
visual.caption: Find the feature, then decide whether it is met.

slides.narration: A tea-shop owner managing staff in her own way shows art. A chain testing two shift patterns and keeping the better one shows the method of science. A hotel appointing a manager without a degree shows that management is not a full profession. A bonus that works in one city and fails in another shows an inexact science.

slides.heading: Quick check: testing layouts
slides.body_md: A candle maker tried three packing-room layouts, recorded output and kept the best. Which feature of science does this show?
slides.narration: How do scientists arrive at their principles?

slides.heading: The verdict
columns:
**Yes**

Management is an art and an inexact science.

**Not yet**

Management is not a full profession, though it is moving that way.

rows: Not fully; it is moving that way

visual.alt: Verdict table: management is an inexact science, an art, and not yet a full profession

slides.narration: So what is the verdict? Management is both an art and a science, but an inexact science because it deals with people. It is not yet a full profession, since entry is open and codes are not binding, but it is moving in that direction as more managers are trained formally.

slides.heading: Why management matters

rows: Every crew member works towards finishing repairs before the season
A potter's kiln schedule saves firewood
Weavers adopt new yarns as tastes change
Fair pay and recognition keep staff motivated
Helps in the development of society
Better goods, more jobs, new technology

visual.alt: Table of five points of importance of management, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: Management matters in five ways. It helps a group achieve its goals by uniting individual efforts. It increases efficiency by cutting waste. It creates a dynamic organisation that adapts to change. It helps meet the personal objectives of staff. And it helps develop society, through better goods, more jobs and new technology.

slides.heading: Quick check: adapting to change
slides.body_md: A manager persuades senior weavers to try new yarns as buyers ask for light summer saris. Which importance of management is this?
slides.narration: Is the firm standing still, or changing with its market?

slides.heading: Levels of management
slides.body_md: Managers are arranged in **three levels**, joined by a chain of authority.

Operative workers below are managed, not managers
visual.caption: Three levels of management, from the board down to the shop floor.

slides.narration: In most organisations, managers work at three levels. At the top are the board and the chief executive. In the middle are department, plant and regional heads. At the base are supervisors and foremen who work directly with the workers. The workers themselves are managed, but they are not managers.

slides.heading: What each level does

rows: Frame goals and strategy; read the environment; answerable for survival and welfare
Interpret policies; assign duties to supervisors; coordinate departments; motivate
Oversee workers; keep quality and discipline; pass problems upward

visual.alt: Table of the three levels of management, who belongs to each and their main functions

slides.narration: Top managers read the environment, set goals and strategy, and are answerable for the survival of the whole firm. Middle managers interpret those policies, assign duties to supervisors, coordinate departments and motivate their teams. Supervisors oversee the workers, keep quality and discipline, and carry workers' problems upward.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who is at which level?
slides.body_md: Four people work at an imagined cashew processor in Odisha.
bullets: Step 1: ask whether the person **sets goals**, **turns them into plans**, or **watches the work directly**.
Step 2: name the level.
Step 3: remember that workers are not managers.

headers: Imagined person at a cashew processor in Odisha
rows: Directors who decide to double capacity
Factory manager who sets yearly targets for each shed
Shed supervisor who guides shellers each day

visual.alt: Worked table placing four imagined people at a cashew processor at their level of management
visual.caption: Ask: does the person set goals, turn them into plans, or watch the work directly?

slides.narration: Directors who decide to double capacity are setting goals, so they are top management. The factory manager who sets yearly targets for each shed turns goals into plans, so he is middle management. The shed supervisor who guides workers daily is supervisory. The sheller who runs the machine is an operative, not a manager.

slides.heading: Quick check: time at each level
slides.body_md: True or false: a top manager usually spends more time on planning and less on day-to-day supervision than a supervisor does.
slides.narration: Think about what fills the day of a director and of a foreman.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Inexact science; an art; not yet a full profession
Group goals, efficiency, dynamic firm, personal objectives, society
More planning at the top; more supervising at the bottom

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: science, art and profession; importance; levels; and how managers at each level use their time

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Management is an art and an inexact science, and not yet a full profession. It helps achieve group goals, raises efficiency, keeps the firm dynamic, meets personal objectives and develops society. Its three levels are top, middle and supervisory, each with its own functions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For science, art or profession, **test each feature** and give a verdict.
Learn **two functions** for each level.
In level cases, ask: **goals, plans or direct supervision**?
Never call a worker a manager.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the line, name the idea, and explain the link

slides.narration: Final tips. When asked whether management is a science, art or profession, test each feature and end with a clear verdict. Learn at least two functions for each level. In a case, decide whether the person sets goals, turns them into plans, or watches the work directly. And remember that workers are not a level of management.

notes.title: Nature and Significance of Management — notes

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of management
sections.body_md:
**Management** is the process of getting things done **effectively** (on time, meeting the goal) and **efficiently** (at least cost) through others.

The word is used in four senses:
- **As an activity:** what managers do — **interpersonal** (dealing with people), **informational** (receiving and passing on information) and **decisional** (taking decisions) tasks.
- **As a group:** the **body of persons** who manage an organisation, from directors to supervisors.
- **As a discipline:** an **organised field of study** with its own concepts and principles, taught in schools and colleges.
- **As a process:** a **chain of inter-related functions** — planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling — performed to reach goals.

key_terms.definition_md: The process of getting things done effectively and efficiently through others.
Completing the right task on time.
Doing the task at the least cost of resources.

rows: What managers do: interpersonal, informational and decisional tasks
The body of persons who manage an organisation
An organised field of study with its own principles
A chain of functions: plan, organise, staff, direct, control
How work moves from idea to result

sections.heading: 2. Objectives of management
sections.body_md:
- **Organisational objectives:** **survival** (earning enough to cover costs and stay in business), **profit** (a surplus over costs to reward owners and fund growth) and **growth** (expanding sales, capacity, products or markets).
- **Social objectives:** creating benefit for society — quality products at fair prices, eco-friendly methods, jobs for disadvantaged groups, support to the community.
- **Personal objectives:** meeting the varied needs of employees — **financial** (fair pay), **social** (recognition by peers) and **higher-level** (personal growth and development).

A good manager balances all three kinds.

key_terms.definition_md: Survival, profit and growth of the firm.
Benefits the firm creates for society.
Meeting the financial, social and higher-level needs of employees.

rows: A trekking firm cuts costs to stay open in a bad year
Benefit to society: safe products, jobs, clean environment
A seafood exporter treats its waste water
Employees' financial, social and higher-level needs
A spice firm pays for evening classes for workers

sections.heading: 3. Characteristics of management
sections.body_md:
- **Goal-oriented:** all management work aims at definite objectives; success is judged by how far they are met.
- **Pervasive:** management is needed in all organisations — business or not, large or small — and at every level.
- **Continuous:** its functions are performed again and again; controlling leads into fresh planning.
- **Group activity:** an organisation is a group of individuals with different needs; management unites their efforts towards common goals.
- **Intangible:** management cannot be seen or touched, but its presence is felt in orderly work, met targets and satisfied people.

key_terms.definition_md: Found in every kind of organisation and at every level.
Cannot be seen, though its effects can be felt.

Its functions repeat without a break
Unites people with different needs towards common goals
Cannot be seen, but its results can be felt

sections.heading: 4. Management as a science, an art and a profession
sections.body_md:
**Science** — features: systematised body of knowledge; principles based on observation and experiment; universal validity. Management has organised knowledge and tested principles, but because they deal with human behaviour they do not hold exactly everywhere: an **inexact (soft) science**.

**Art** — features: existence of theoretical knowledge; personalised application; based on practice and creativity. Management meets all three: it is an **art**.

**Profession** — features: well-defined body of knowledge; restricted entry; professional association; ethical code; service motive. Management has a body of knowledge, but entry is **not restricted**, association membership is **not compulsory**, and no code is binding by law: **not a full profession**.

**Verdict:** management is both an art and an inexact science, and it is moving towards becoming a profession.

key_terms.definition_md: A science whose principles do not give identical results everywhere because they deal with people.
Entry to an occupation only through a set degree, examination or licence.

Yes, though people cannot be tested like chemicals
Only partly: results vary with people and situations

sections.heading: 5. Importance of management
sections.body_md:
- **Helps achieve group goals:** it directs individual efforts towards the common goals of the organisation.
- **Increases efficiency:** better planning, organising and control reduce waste and cost.
- **Creates a dynamic organisation:** it helps people accept and adapt to change.
- **Helps achieve personal objectives:** through fair pay, recognition and growth.
- **Helps in the development of society:** through quality goods, jobs, new technology and responsible use of resources.

key_terms.definition_md: One that keeps adapting to changes in its environment.

rows: Every crew member works towards finishing repairs before the season
A potter's kiln schedule saves firewood
Weavers adopt new yarns as tastes change
Fair pay and recognition keep staff motivated
Helps in the development of society
Better goods, more jobs, new technology

visual.alt: Table of five points of importance of management, each with an imagined example

sections.heading: 6. Levels of management and their functions
sections.body_md:
**Top management** (board, chief executive, directors): analyses the environment; frames overall objectives and strategies; arranges resources; is answerable for the survival and welfare of the whole organisation.

**Middle management** (department, plant and regional heads): interprets the policies of top management; assigns duties to supervisors; ensures enough staff and resources; coordinates departments; motivates supervisors.

**Supervisory (lower) management** (foremen, line supervisors): oversees workers directly; keeps quality and discipline; passes workers' problems upward and managers' instructions downward; guides and trains workers.

**Time:** planning takes more of a top manager's time; direct supervision takes more of a supervisor's. Operative workers are managed but are **not** a level of management.

key_terms.definition_md: The highest level, which sets goals and strategy.
The link between top and supervisory managers.
The level in direct contact with workers.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up pervasive (found everywhere) with continuous (never stops).
- Calling management a full profession, or an exact science.
- Listing jobs for disadvantaged groups as a personal objective (it is social).
- Treating operative workers as a level of management.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: the correct option, sense, objective or level.
- 2–3 marks: each point named and explained, linked to the case.
- 5 marks: parts answered separately; science, art and profession questions need each feature tested and a verdict.
- Case questions: quote the line, name the idea, explain the link.

cards.back_md: Getting things done effectively and efficiently through others.

cards.front_md: Four senses of the word management
cards.back_md: Activity, group, discipline, process.
Interpersonal, informational and decisional tasks of managers.
The body of persons who manage an organisation.
An organised field of study with its own principles.
Planning → organising → staffing → directing → controlling.
Effective: the goal is met on time. Efficient: at least cost.
Survival, profit, growth.
Benefits to society: safe products, jobs, clean environment.
Employees' financial, social and higher-level needs.
Goal-oriented, pervasive, continuous, group activity, intangible.
Needed in every kind of organisation and at every level.
Cannot be seen; felt through its results.
Functions repeat without a break.
Systematised knowledge; experiment-based principles; universal validity.
Its principles deal with people, so results vary.
Theory exists; personalised application; practice and creativity.
Body of knowledge, restricted entry, association, ethical code, service motive.

cards.front_md: Which profession feature does management fully meet?
cards.back_md: Only a well-defined body of knowledge.

cards.front_md: Verdict on the nature of management
cards.back_md: An art and an inexact science; not yet a full profession.
Group goals, efficiency, dynamic organisation, personal objectives, development of society.
Management increases efficiency.
Management creates a dynamic organisation.
Top, middle, supervisory (lower).
Frames goals and strategy; answerable for survival and welfare.
Interprets policies, assigns duties, coordinates, motivates.
Oversees workers; quality and discipline; passes problems upward.
Most at the top; least at the supervisory level.

cards.front_md: Are workers a level of management?
cards.back_md: No: they are managed, not managers.
Quote the line, name the idea, explain the link.

questions.stem_md: On their first morning, new supervisors at the imagined Lonavla Chikki Works are told that their job runs as a chain: decide the week's targets, arrange people and machines, fill vacancies, guide the team and then compare results with the targets. In this talk, management is being described as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a process. A series of inter-related functions (planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling) carried out one after another is management seen as a process.

questions.stem_md: A notice on the canteen board of the imagined Hampi Stoneware reads: "The management has approved two extra holidays for the harvest festival." Here the word management refers to

options.text_md: the series of functions such as planning and controlling
the personal skill of one manager
the group of persons who manage the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the group of persons who manage the firm. The notice speaks of the people in charge who took a decision, so management is used in the sense of a group (the body of managers).

questions.stem_md: Farida, a commerce graduate from Bhopal, joins an imagined two-year course where she reads case studies, learns principles of running organisations and writes a research project. For Farida, management is

options.text_md: a discipline, that is, a field of study
an activity of decision making on a shop floor
a profession with compulsory entry rules

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a discipline, that is, a field of study. An organised body of knowledge that is taught and studied is management as a discipline.

questions.stem_md: The manager of the imagined Majuli Mask Studio spends one day meeting a museum buyer, passing on news of a craft fair to the artisans and deciding which of three orders to accept. Seen as interpersonal, informational and decisional tasks, this shows management as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an activity. Meeting people (interpersonal), passing on news (informational) and choosing between orders (decisional) are the things managers do: management as an activity.

questions.stem_md: Management as a discipline means the organised body of knowledge about managing that is taught and studied in schools and colleges.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. As a discipline, management is a field of study with its own concepts, principles and literature.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. "The management has declared a bonus" : management as a group :: "My sister is doing a degree in management" : management as a ___
questions.solution_md: The first sentence refers to the people in charge (a group); the second refers to a subject one studies, that is, a discipline.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Management is often described as a process.

**Reason (R):** It is made up of a series of inter-related functions such as planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the chain of linked functions is exactly what makes management a process.

questions.stem_md: Match each sentence heard at an imagined tea-garden office in Darjeeling with the sense in which it uses the word management.

options.text_md: "Our management has decided to open a tasting room."
"Management is my favourite subject at college."
"Plan, organise, staff, direct and control: that is management."
"Most of a manager's day goes in meeting people, sharing news and taking decisions."

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). People in charge form a group; a subject of study is a discipline; a chain of functions is a process; what managers do every day is an activity.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of management as a group and as a discipline.
questions.solution_md: Each sense explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **As a group:** management means the **body of persons** who manage an organisation, from the board and chief executive down to supervisors, as in "the management has decided".
2. **As a discipline:** it is an **organised field of study** with its own principles, taught in schools and colleges.

questions.stem_md: Tsering runs the imagined Dhauladhar Trekking Company. Using her work as the example, explain management as an activity, giving one example each of an interpersonal, an informational and a decisional activity.
questions.solution_md: One example of each kind of activity, linked to the trekking firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Interpersonal activity:** Tsering **meets guides, porters and clients**, leads the team and settles quarrels on the trail.
2. **Informational activity:** she **collects weather and permit news** and **passes it on** to guides and trekkers before each trip.
3. **Decisional activity:** she **decides** whether a trek goes ahead in bad weather, which routes to offer and how to share the budget.

questions.stem_md: A youth club runs an imagined village library near Nalanda. Explain management as a process by showing how three of its functions would be carried out at the library.
questions.solution_md: Management as a chain of functions, with three functions applied to the library.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Planning:** the club **decides in advance** to lend 300 books a month and to open on Sunday mornings.
2. **Organising and staffing:** it **divides tasks** such as issuing books and repairing covers, and **picks volunteers** suited to each task.
3. **Controlling:** at the end of each month it **compares** books actually lent with the target and finds the reasons for any shortfall. Each function leads into the next.

marking_scheme.step: Third function applied with the link between them

questions.stem_md: After two seasons of landslides kept tourists away, the imagined Dhauladhar Trekking Company cut its costs, rented out its tents and earned just enough to cover its expenses and stay open. Which objective of management did it put first?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Survival, an organisational objective. Earning enough to cover costs and remain in business is the organisational objective of survival.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Chilika Prawn Exports buys only from fishers who respect the closed breeding season, treats its waste water before release and runs an evening school for fishers' children. These steps serve which objective of management?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Social objectives. Using eco-friendly methods and giving back to the community are social objectives: creating benefit for society.

questions.stem_md: Each month the imagined Coorg Pepper House names a "grader of the month", pays for evening computer classes for workers who want them, and revises wages every year in line with prices. These policies serve mainly the
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** personal objectives of management. Fair pay (financial needs), recognition (social needs) and chances to learn (higher-level needs) meet the personal objectives of employees.

questions.stem_md:
The owner of the imagined Bhimtal Candles lists four aims for the next three years:
P. Earn enough to stay in business through the slack summer months.
Q. Open two more shops in nearby hill towns.
R. Give jobs to women from nearby villages.
S. Earn a surplus over costs to reward the owners.
Which of these are **organisational** objectives?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** P, Q and S. Survival (P), growth (Q) and profit (S) are organisational objectives. Jobs for women from villages (R) is a social objective.

questions.stem_md: A community kitchen in Amritsar, a ferry cooperative in Goa and a chip-design start-up in Hyderabad (all imagined) each plan their work, divide tasks and check results. Which characteristic of management does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is pervasive. Management is needed in every kind of organisation, business or not, and at every level: it is pervasive (universal).

questions.stem_md: No runner at the imagined Sinhagad Ridge Half Marathon ever sees the organising committee at work, yet everyone notices that water points are stocked in time, signs are clear and results appear within an hour. Which characteristic of management is shown?

options.text_md: Management is a group of people

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Management is intangible. Management cannot be seen or touched; its presence is felt through orderly work and results. It is intangible.

questions.stem_md: The manager of the imagined Bhimtal Candles finishes the Diwali sales plan, reviews the November results and at once begins planning for the Christmas and New Year orders. This shows that management is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a continuous process. The functions of management are performed again and again without a break: management is a continuous process.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Pochampally Ikat House, dyers, weavers, accountants and sales staff each have their own needs, yet the manager gets them all to work together on one large export order. Which characteristic of management does this show best?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Management is a group activity. An organisation is a collection of individuals with different needs; management unites their efforts towards common goals, so it is a group activity.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Pochampally Ikat House opens a showroom in Bengaluru, doubles its looms and adds a range of cushion covers. Which objective of management is it pursuing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Growth, an organisational objective. Expanding sales, capacity and the product range shows the organisational objective of growth.

questions.stem_md: Management is needed only in organisations that aim to earn a profit.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Management is pervasive: schools, hospitals, clubs and government offices need it as much as business firms do.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Management is a goal-oriented process.

**Reason (R):** Management is intangible, as it cannot be seen or touched.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but intangibility does not explain why management is goal-oriented; it is goal-oriented because all its activities aim at the organisation's objectives.

questions.stem_md: Because management is intangible, its effect on an organisation cannot be noticed in any way.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Management cannot be seen or touched, but its presence is felt through results such as orderly work, met targets and satisfied staff.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Earning a surplus over costs : organisational objective :: Supplying safe products to the community : ___ objective
questions.solution_md: Profit is an organisational objective; supplying safe products for the good of society is a social objective.

questions.stem_md: An imagined private bus company in Shillong wants to meet its social objectives. Suggest two steps it could take, and say why each is a social objective.
questions.solution_md: Two suitable steps, each linked to benefit for society.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Running buses on time on remote village routes** even when few passengers travel, because it **serves the community** and not only the firm.
2. **Keeping engines well tuned to cut smoke**, because it **protects the environment** that society shares.

questions.stem_md: What are the personal objectives of management? Name the kinds of needs of employees they cover.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus the three kinds of needs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Personal objectives** are the aims of meeting the **varied needs of the people** who work in the organisation. They cover **financial needs** (fair pay), **social needs** (recognition by peers) and **higher-level needs** (personal growth and development).

questions.stem_md: Explain these three characteristics of management: it is goal-oriented, it is pervasive and it is continuous.
questions.solution_md: Each characteristic explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Goal-oriented:** every management activity aims at **definite objectives**, such as a sales or output target; success is judged by how far these are met.
2. **Pervasive:** management is needed in **all organisations**, business or non-business, large or small, and at all levels.
3. **Continuous:** its functions are performed **again and again**; one cycle of planning to controlling leads straight into the next.

questions.stem_md: Chilika Prawn Exports (imagined) wants to balance all three kinds of objectives of management. Suggest one suitable step for each kind, explaining why it fits that kind.
questions.solution_md: One suitable step for each kind of objective, with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Organisational:** fix **prices above costs** and enter one new export market, so the firm can **survive, earn profit and grow**.
2. **Social:** **treat waste water** before release and buy only from fishers who respect the breeding season, which **protects the lake** and the community.
3. **Personal:** pay **fair wages on time** and train packers to become supervisors, meeting **employees' needs** for income and growth.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Pasighat Riverbank Music Festival in Arunachal Pradesh is run by a committee of volunteers. Explain five characteristics of management, illustrating each with an example from the festival.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each characteristic explained with a festival example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Goal-oriented:** all work aims at clear goals, such as **holding three days of music safely within the budget**.
2. **Pervasive:** although the festival is **not a business**, it still needs planning, organising and control, so management is found everywhere.
3. **Continuous:** once one festival ends, the committee **reviews it and starts planning next year's**, so the cycle never stops.
4. **Group activity:** sound engineers, cooks, guides and ticket sellers have **different needs** but work towards **one shared event**.
5. **Intangible:** visitors never see "the management", but they **feel its presence** in clean campsites, timely shows and smooth entry.

questions.stem_md: Tsering of the imagined Dhauladhar Trekking Company has read the same books on leading teams as other trek leaders, but her way of calming a tired and angry group at high camp is her own, sharpened over ten seasons. This shows management as

options.text_md: a science: principles with universal validity
a profession: restricted entry and a compulsory code
a discipline: a subject taught in colleges
an art: personal skill used creatively and improved by practice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an art: personal skill used creatively and improved by practice. Personalised application of knowledge, creativity and skill improved through practice are features of an art.

questions.stem_md: A bonus scheme that raised output sharply at the Hospet unit of the imagined Hampi Stoneware had almost no effect at its Mysuru unit. This is one reason why management is described as

options.text_md: a purely personal art with no principles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an inexact (soft) science. Management principles deal with human behaviour, which varies, so they do not give the same result everywhere; management is an inexact science.

questions.stem_md: Before choosing a layout for its packing room, the imagined Bhimtal Candles tried three arrangements for a week each, recorded the output and kept the best one. Which feature of science does this show in management?

options.text_md: Principles based on observation and experiment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Principles based on observation and experiment. Science develops principles through observation and repeated experiment, and management does the same when it tests and records results.

questions.stem_md:
A debate club at an imagined school in Kohima lists four features of a profession:
P. A well-defined body of knowledge.
Q. Entry only through a compulsory degree or licence.
R. Membership of a professional association required by law.
S. A code of conduct whose breach can cost a member the right to practise.
Which of these does management in India **fully** satisfy today?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** P only. Management has a well-defined, systematised body of knowledge (P). Anyone may become a manager without a set degree (Q not met); membership of a managers' association is not compulsory (R not met); and there is no legally binding code that can stop a person managing (S not met).

questions.stem_md: A student at an imagined coaching class in Kota writes that management has "a systematised body of knowledge with principles based on cause and effect". He is describing management as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a science. A systematised body of knowledge and cause-and-effect principles are features of a science.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Management can be described as an art.

**Reason (R):** Management principles give exactly the same result in every situation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true: managers apply knowledge with personal skill and creativity. The reason is false: management principles deal with human behaviour and do not give identical results everywhere.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Management principles are as exact as the laws of physics.

**Reason (R):** In India, a person needs a licence issued under law before working as a manager.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Management principles are flexible guidelines about human behaviour, not exact laws; and there is no legal licence needed to work as a manager in India.

questions.stem_md: In India, a person must by law hold a management degree before being appointed as a manager of a company.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. There is no legal restriction on entry; a person with any qualification may be appointed a manager, which is why management is not a full profession.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Personalised application of knowledge : art :: Principles based on cause and effect : ___
questions.solution_md: Personal skill in applying knowledge is a feature of art; cause-and-effect principles are a feature of science.

questions.stem_md: State two features of an art that are present in management.
questions.solution_md: Any two features of art (existence of theoretical knowledge, personalised application, practice and creativity) explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Personalised application:** each manager **applies** the same principles **in an individual way**, with her own style.
2. **Based on practice and creativity:** managerial skill **improves with practice**, and good managers find **creative** new ways to solve problems.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why management is not yet regarded as a full profession in India.
questions.solution_md: Two unmet features of a profession explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No restricted entry:** **anyone** can be appointed a manager; no degree or licence is required by law.
2. **No compulsory association or binding code:** joining a managers' association is **voluntary**, and its code of conduct cannot stop a person from working as a manager.

questions.stem_md: Ananya, a Class 12 student, tells her friend: "Management is a science, just like chemistry." Using three features of science, examine how far she is right.
questions.solution_md: Three features of science tested against management, ending with a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Systematised body of knowledge:** management **does** have organised principles and theories, so she is partly right.
2. **Principles based on experiment:** its principles come from **observation and testing** in many firms, though tests on people cannot be fully controlled.
3. **Universal validity:** management principles **do not give the same result everywhere**, because they deal with human behaviour. So management is only an **inexact (soft) science**, not exact like chemistry.

questions.stem_md: Using three features of a profession, evaluate whether the manager of an imagined hotel in Udaipur can be called a professional in the full sense.
questions.solution_md: Three features of a profession evaluated with a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Body of knowledge:** **met** — management has a well-defined body of knowledge that the manager can learn.
2. **Restricted entry:** **not met** — the hotel may appoint **anyone** as manager; no compulsory degree or licence is required by law.
3. **Professional association and code:** **not fully met** — joining a managers' association is **voluntary**, and its code cannot stop a member from working. So the manager is **not yet** a professional in the full sense.

questions.stem_md:
Kiran, who runs the imagined Hampi Stoneware, says: "I never studied management, yet my unit runs well. So management is just an art; it is neither a science nor a profession."
(a) Explain two features of an art that support Kiran. [2]
(b) Evaluate his claim that management is neither a science nor a profession. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two features of art; a balanced evaluation of science and profession with a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Personalised application:** Kiran uses his **own style** to apply ideas, much like a musician interprets a raga. **Practice and creativity:** his skill has **grown through years of practice** and fresh solutions on the shop floor.

(b) **Science:** Kiran is **only partly right**. Management has a **systematised body of knowledge** and principles drawn from observation, but because they deal with people they are not universally exact, so it is an **inexact science**.
**Profession:** he is **largely right**. There is a body of knowledge, but **entry is not restricted**, membership of an association is **not compulsory** and no legal code binds managers. So management is **not a full profession**.
**Conclusion:** management is **both an art and an inexact science**, and it is moving towards becoming a profession.

questions.stem_md: After a new manager took charge at the imagined Lonavla Chikki Works, wastage of jaggery fell, each worker got clear duties and a new range of sugar-free chikki was launched. Which of the following is **not** an importance of management shown here?

options.text_md: It increases efficiency by reducing waste
It guarantees that the firm will never suffer a loss
It helps the group achieve its goals
It creates a dynamic organisation that adapts to change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It guarantees that the firm will never suffer a loss. Less waste shows efficiency, clear duties help achieve group goals, and the new range shows a dynamic organisation. No management can guarantee that a firm will never make a loss.

questions.stem_md: After the new manager of the imagined Hampi Stoneware fixed a kiln-loading schedule, the firewood used for each batch of pots fell by a quarter with no fall in output. Which importance of management does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It increases efficiency. Getting the same output with fewer inputs means lower cost per unit: management increases efficiency.

questions.stem_md: When buyers began asking for light cotton saris for summer, the manager of the imagined Pochampally Ikat House persuaded senior weavers, who had always used heavy silk, to try new yarns. Which importance of management does this show?

options.text_md: It helps create a dynamic organisation
It helps achieve personal objectives only
It reduces the need for planning
It makes the organisation static and stable

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It helps create a dynamic organisation. Management helps people accept change and adapt to new conditions, keeping the organisation dynamic.

questions.stem_md: The board and the managing director of the imagined Chilika Prawn Exports decide to start exporting to Japan within two years and set aside funds for a new freezing plant. Which level of management is at work?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Top management. Setting long-term goals and allocating funds for the whole firm is the work of top management.

questions.stem_md: Joseph heads the grading plant of the imagined Coorg Pepper House. He turns the board's yearly target into monthly quotas for each shift, gives duties to the shift supervisors and reports progress to the directors. Joseph belongs to
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** middle management. Interpreting policies of the top, assigning duties to supervisors and reporting upward are middle-management functions.

questions.stem_md: Lalremruati is a line in-charge at an imagined bamboo-blind factory in Aizawl. She checks each worker's daily output, settles small quarrels, shows new hands the correct cutting method and passes workers' complaints upward. Her level of management is

options.text_md: none: she is an operative worker

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** supervisory (lower) management. Directly overseeing workers, maintaining quality and discipline, and passing their problems up are supervisory functions.

questions.stem_md:
Which of the following are functions of **middle** management in an imagined cement company?
P. Interpreting the policies framed by top management.
Q. Assigning duties to the plant supervisors.
R. Deciding the long-term goals of the whole company.
S. Ensuring cooperation among departments and motivating supervisors.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** P, Q and S. Interpreting policies (P), assigning duties (Q) and securing cooperation and motivation (S) are middle-management tasks. Long-term goals (R) are set by top management.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Top management is responsible for the welfare and survival of the whole organisation.

**Reason (R):** Top managers analyse the business environment and frame the overall objectives and strategies of the firm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because top managers read the environment and frame overall goals and strategies, they are answerable for the survival and welfare of the whole organisation.

questions.stem_md: A top manager usually spends more time on planning and less time on day-to-day supervision of workers than a first-line supervisor does.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Planning takes a larger share of a top manager's time, while a supervisor spends most of the day guiding and overseeing workers.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Board of directors and chief executive : top management :: Foremen and line supervisors : ___ management
questions.solution_md: Directors and the chief executive form top management; foremen and line supervisors form supervisory (lower) management.

questions.stem_md: Match each task at an imagined chain of hill-station hotels with the level of management that usually performs it.

options.text_md: Decide to open a new hotel in Gangtok within three years
Turn the chain's yearly room-booking target into targets for each hotel
Check that each room on a floor is cleaned before guests arrive
Make the beds and serve breakfast to guests

match_right.text_md: Operative staff, not a level of management

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A new hotel is a top-level decision; turning targets into unit plans is middle management; checking rooms each day is supervisory work; making beds and serving guests is operative work done under supervisors.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the supervisory level of management at an imagined granite-polishing unit in Ongole.
questions.solution_md: Two supervisory functions linked to the polishing unit.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Overseeing workers:** the supervisor **checks daily output** of the polishers and makes sure the right method is used.
2. **Link between workers and middle management:** she **passes workers' problems upward** and explains the instructions of managers to them.

questions.stem_md: Before a manager was appointed at an imagined ferry service in Goa, boats left late and fuel was wasted. State two ways in which good management could help this service.
questions.solution_md: Two points of importance linked to the ferry service.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Increases efficiency:** proper **schedules and fuel checks** cut waste and lower costs.
2. **Helps achieve group goals:** clear duties for crew and ticket staff make everyone work towards **on-time departures** and satisfied passengers.

marking_scheme.step: First point linked to the case
Second point linked to the case

questions.stem_md: Meghna has just been promoted to head the sales team of an imagined spice company for the whole of eastern India, with six area supervisors under her. Explain three functions she will perform at her new level.
questions.solution_md: Three middle-management functions applied to Meghna's post.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Interpreting policies:** she turns the **company's yearly sales policy** into plans and targets for each area.
2. **Assigning duties:** she **divides the work** among the six area supervisors and gives them the resources they need.
3. **Cooperation and motivation:** she **coordinates** with the warehouse and accounts teams, and **motivates** supervisors to meet targets. She is in **middle management**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which management is important not only to a firm but also to society.
questions.solution_md: Three points of importance for society explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Development of society:** well-managed firms supply **better goods and services**, create **jobs** and adopt new technology, raising living standards.
2. **Efficient use of resources:** management **reduces waste** of scarce materials, money and labour, which benefits the whole economy.
3. **Meeting social objectives:** it helps firms act responsibly, for example by **protecting the environment** and serving the community.

questions.stem_md:
At the imagined Konark Cashew Processors in Odisha, the chief executive and directors decide to double capacity in three years; the factory manager turns this into yearly targets for each shed; and four shed supervisors guide the shelling and packing workers each day.
(a) Identify the three levels of management in the case. [1]
(b) Explain two functions of each of the top and middle levels in this firm. [4]
questions.solution_md: Three levels identified; two functions each for top and middle management applied to the firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Top:** chief executive and directors; **middle:** factory manager; **supervisory:** the four shed supervisors.

(b) **Top management:**
1. **Frames long-term goals and strategy**, such as doubling capacity in three years, after studying the market and environment.
2. **Arranges resources** for the plan, such as funds for new sheds, and is answerable for the firm's **survival and welfare**.

**Middle management:**
1. **Interprets** the directors' plan and turns it into **yearly targets for each shed**.
2. **Assigns duties** to the shed supervisors, gives them the materials they need and **coordinates** with purchase and sales so that targets are met.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined Kuttanad Boat Clinic repairs houseboats in Kerala. Its owner says that hiring a trained manager last year "changed everything".
(a) Explain four points of importance of management that could explain this change, with an example of each from the boat clinic. [4]
(b) State one personal objective the manager should pursue for the repair crew. [1]
questions.solution_md: Four points of importance with boat-clinic examples; one personal objective.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Achieving group goals:** the manager gives every crew member a clear role, so the team works towards **finishing repairs before the tourist season**.
2. **Increasing efficiency:** better **scheduling of boats and tools** cuts idle time and wastage of timber and paint.
3. **Creating a dynamic organisation:** the manager helps the crew learn **fibreglass repair** as owners move away from wooden hulls.
4. **Achieving personal objectives:** fair pay and recognition keep skilled carpenters **motivated** and loyal.

(b) **Training and growth:** sending crew members on a **short course in engine repair**, so they earn more and develop their skills.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined firm and people, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (d)** Social objective. Benefiting the community by keeping its craft alive is a social objective.

**(b)** People with different interests working towards a common goal: group activity.

**(c) (i)** Two kinds of activity with the matching words.

**OR (c) (ii)** Survival and growth identified with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) Social objective

**(b)** **Management is a group activity.**

**(c) (i)** 1. **Interpersonal activity:** "**meeting buyers**".
2. **Decisional activity:** "**deciding which orders to accept**".

**OR (c) (ii)** **Survival:** "earn enough to keep twelve artisans in work all year" means staying in business. **Growth:** "grow into online sales" means expanding the business.

questions.passage_md:
**Majuli Mask Studio (imagined), Assam**

Majuli Mask Studio makes painted bamboo masks for theatres and tourists. Its manager, Pranjal, spends his mornings meeting buyers and his afternoons deciding which orders to accept. The studio aims to earn enough to keep twelve artisans in work all year, to grow into online sales, and to keep the craft alive by training young people from the island free of charge. When a large order came from a theatre in Kolkata, carvers, painters and packers, each with different interests, worked together to finish it on time.

children.stem_md: Training young islanders free of charge to keep the craft alive serves which objective of the studio?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Social objective. Benefiting the community by keeping its craft alive is a social objective.

children.stem_md: Name the characteristic of management shown when carvers, painters and packers worked together on the theatre order.
children.solution_md: People with different interests working towards a common goal: group activity.

answer.model_answer_md: **Management is a group activity.**

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify two kinds of managerial activity performed by Pranjal, quoting the words that show each.
children.solution_md: Two kinds of activity with the matching words.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Interpersonal activity:** "**meeting buyers**".
2. **Decisional activity:** "**deciding which orders to accept**".

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Identify two organisational objectives of the studio from the passage, with reasons.
alternatives.solution_md: Survival and growth identified with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: **Survival:** "earn enough to keep twelve artisans in work all year" means staying in business. **Growth:** "grow into online sales" means expanding the business.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined organisation and people, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (b)** Middle management. Turning top-level decisions into schedules and dividing work among supervisors is middle management.

**(b)** Any one supervisory function from the passage.

**(c) (i)** The line about personal style, explained as personalised application.

**OR (c) (ii)** Restricted entry identified and explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) Middle management

**(b)** **Overseeing trainees** in the water and correcting their stance (or reporting injuries upward).

**(c) (i)** "**each coach in the school teaches in a personal style**": an art involves the **personalised application** of knowledge, using one's own skill and creativity.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Restricted entry** is missing: he manages without a **management degree or licence**, as no law restricts who may become a manager.

questions.passage_md:
**Blue Tide Surf School (imagined), Varkala**

The surf school has a founder-director, a head coach and three beach supervisors. The founder decides each year how many batches to run and whether to open a second beach. The head coach turns these decisions into weekly schedules and divides the trainees among the supervisors. Each supervisor watches the trainees in the water, corrects their stance and reports injuries. The head coach has no management degree but has trained hundreds of surfers, and each coach in the school teaches in a personal style.

children.stem_md: The head coach in the passage belongs to which level of management?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Middle management. Turning top-level decisions into schedules and dividing work among supervisors is middle management.

children.stem_md: State one function of the beach supervisors mentioned in the passage.
children.solution_md: Any one supervisory function from the passage.

answer.model_answer_md: **Overseeing trainees** in the water and correcting their stance (or reporting injuries upward).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which line shows management as an art? Explain why.
children.solution_md: The line about personal style, explained as personalised application.

answer.model_answer_md: "**each coach in the school teaches in a personal style**": an art involves the **personalised application** of knowledge, using one's own skill and creativity.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which feature of a profession is missing in the head coach's case? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: **Restricted entry** is missing: he manages without a **management degree or licence**, as no law restricts who may become a manager.
